title: Needs and wants
job: Say what you want and don't want
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The first case ending you write yourself: a feminine noun ending in -а or -я swaps that ending for -у or -ю when it is the thing being wanted, liked or taken. вода → воду, книга → книгу, музыка → музыку. Nothing else in the sentence moves.

The object does NOT always change, and M1 showed you why before this rule existed: a masculine noun naming a thing rather than a living creature (чай, хлеб, сок) looks identical whether it is the subject or the object, a neuter noun (молоко) likewise, and кофе never changes at all. So "the object case changes the ending" is only true of the feminine -а/-я nouns at this level. Learn which nouns move rather than expecting all of them to.

Negation is one word in one place: не goes immediately in front of the verb and nothing else happens. Я не хочу кофе. English has to fetch an auxiliary — do not, does not, did not — and Russian has nothing of the kind, in any tense. This one word will still be doing the whole job in M5's past and M6's future.
Wanting to DO something is хочу plus the plain dictionary form of the verb, with no word for "to": Я хочу работать. English's "to" tempts a что or a чтобы into the gap, and neither belongs there.

хотеть does not follow either of the ordinary ending patterns — it is one of a handful of Russian verbs that mix them: хочу (I), хочет (he, she), хотите (you, polite). Learn these three shapes as they come; M4 sorts out the verbs that DO behave.

A word borrowed whole from another language often refuses to change at all: кофе is the same in every position in every sentence. There are only a few such nouns, and they are a gift — nothing to learn.

words.note: "I want", from хотеть. This verb mixes the two ending patterns and has to be learned shape by shape: хочу (I), хочет (he or she), хотите (you, polite). It is blunter in Russian than "I want" is in English only when it is bare — adding пожалуйста makes it a perfectly ordinary request.

sentences.trap: Nothing happened to чай. After a whole module about endings it is easy to expect one here — but a masculine thing keeps its dictionary shape as the object, and that is the point of starting with this sentence.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO chai. The х is the raspy h from хорошо, and the о in front of the stress flattens to "a".

variations.changed: swap the drink — another masculine thing, so still nothing moves
хочу → хотите for the polite you, and the sentence becomes a question with nothing added
пожалуйста turns the bare want into a request — the ordinary way to order something

mistake.why: чаю is a real shape of чай, but it belongs to a different job (a partial amount — "some tea"), and this level does not teach it. Я хочу чай.

sentences.usage: Ordering, asking, saying what you would like — add пожалуйста and it is polite anywhere.
sentences.mnemonic: Masculine things that are not alive travel light: subject or object, same shape.

words.note: Water. вода is the dictionary shape and the subject shape; воду is what it becomes as the object of a verb — the first ending in this course you will write on purpose. Note that the stress jumps as the ending changes: va-DA, but VO-doo.

sentences.trap: Я хочу вода is the sentence an English speaker writes, because English objects never change. It is the module's whole lesson in one error: a feminine -а noun becomes -у when it is what you want.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO VO-doo. The stress moves from the ending to the front when вода becomes воду, which is why the two shapes barely sound alike.

variations.changed: не in front of the verb — and the object keeps the ending it already had
the polite you-form as a question, with the object still bent
the verb dropped entirely — and the object keeps its ending, because the verb is still understood

mistake.why: вода is the shape for the subject of a sentence. As the thing wanted it becomes воду.

sentences.usage: Anywhere you would ask for water — a café, a shop, somebody's kitchen.
sentences.mnemonic: -а is the shape that sits still; -у is the shape something is being done to.

words.note: Book. The same swap as вода — feminine -а becomes -у as the object — but here the stress does not move: KNEE-ga, KNEE-goo. Whether the stress jumps is a fact about each word, not a rule, and it has to be picked up word by word.

sentences.trap: Still no word for "a". Я хочу книгу covers "I want a book" and "I want the book" alike, and which one is meant comes from the conversation.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO KNEE-goo. Both к and н are said at the start — Russian is comfortable with the cluster English lost centuries ago.

variations.cue: I would like a book, please
variations.changed: пожалуйста makes it a request rather than a demand
хочу → хочет: the person changes and the object keeps its ending
не in front of the verb, and nothing else moves

mistake.why: The dictionary shape книга is for the subject. As the thing wanted it is книгу.

sentences.usage: In a shop or a library — and the same frame does duty for anything you are asking for.
sentences.mnemonic: Every -а that gets wanted turns into -у.

words.note: "Not", and it goes immediately in front of the word it denies — almost always the verb. Nothing else in the sentence changes and nothing is added: Russian has no do not, does not or did not, in any tense. This one small word will still be doing the whole job in M5's past and M6's future.

Coffee — borrowed whole, and it refuses to change shape in any position in any sentence. It counts as masculine, in spite of the -е ending that usually means neuter; you will hear the neuter used too, and it is still argued about.

sentences.trap: English needs "do" to say no to something — I don't want — and hunting for its Russian equivalent is wasted effort. There is none. не does the whole job on its own.
sentences.sound: ya nye kha-CHOO KO-fye. не leans onto the verb and is barely a syllable of its own.

variations.changed: swap the drink — не stays exactly where it was
drop не and the sentence flips: nothing else has to move back
the person changes; не still sits in front of the verb

mistake.why: That says "it is not coffee that I want" — не denies whatever follows it, so putting it before the noun changes the meaning. To refuse, it goes in front of the verb: Я не хочу кофе.

sentences.usage: Turning something down — and adding спасибо makes it polite rather than blunt.
sentences.mnemonic: не sticks to the front of the verb like a burr; move it and you have said something else.

words.note: Bread. Masculine — it ends in a consonant — and a thing rather than a creature, so it never changes as the object. There is no word for "some" in front of it either.

words.cue: please · you're welcome · here you are
words.note: One word doing three English jobs: "please" when you ask, "you're welcome" when you are thanked, and "here you are" when you hand something over. It is what turns a bare Я хочу … into an ordinary polite request, and it is written off by a comma.

sentences.trap: Я хочу on its own is blunt — closer to "I want" than to "I'd like". пожалуйста is what carries the politeness, so a request that leaves it out is a request that sounds abrupt.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO khlyep pa-ZHA-loo-sta. The final б of хлеб is said as a p — Russian hardens the last consonant of a word — and the й inside пожалуйста disappears in ordinary speech.

variations.changed: drop пожалуйста and the request becomes a bare statement of what you want
the verb dropped entirely — and the object keeps its ending, because the verb is still understood
the polite you-form, asked instead of told

mistake.why: хлеба is a real shape and it belongs to the "some of it" job this level does not teach. The plain object is хлеб.

sentences.usage: The shop, the bakery, the table — the most ordinary request in the language.
sentences.mnemonic: пожалуйста is the whole of Russian politeness in one word — and it goes at the end.

words.note: Music. Feminine, so it takes the -у ending as the object, exactly like вода and книга. The stress stays on the first syllable throughout: MOO-zy-ka, MOO-zy-koo.

sentences.trap: M1 taught люблю with objects that never moved — чай, молоко, русский язык. This is the same verb with a feminine object, and now the ending appears. The verb was never what decided it; the noun always was.
sentences.sound: ya lyoo-BLYOO MOO-zy-koo. Two of Russian's harder sounds in one short sentence: the soft л of люблю and the back ы of музыку.

variations.changed: не in front of the verb — the M3 lesson applied to an M1 verb
люблю → любит: the person changes and музыку keeps its ending
the describing word bends with the noun it describes — русский → русскую

mistake.why: The ending belongs to the noun, not to the verb: any feminine -а noun in the object slot becomes -у, whichever verb put it there.

sentences.usage: Saying what you are fond of — the M1 frame, now with the endings it always needed.
sentences.mnemonic: The verb never decides the ending. The noun does.

words.note: The dictionary shape of "work" — the one that goes straight after хочу with nothing between. Its everyday shapes are работаю (I), работаете (you, polite) and работает (he or she); M4 explains where those endings come from. Almost every Russian verb's dictionary shape ends in -ть like this one.

sentences.trap: There is no word for "to". English "want to work" has three words and Russian has two, and the missing one has no Russian stand-in — не что, не чтобы, nothing.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO ra-BO-tat'. The ь on the end of работать is not a sound: it softens the т, so the word ends in a light "t" rather than a hard one.

variations.changed: swap the activity — any dictionary shape drops straight into the slot
хочу → хочет, and работать does not move: only the first verb ever changes
the polite you-form, as a question

mistake.why: The что is English's "to", smuggled in. Nothing goes between хочу and the dictionary shape: Я хочу работать.

sentences.usage: Plans, wishes and job conversations — the most productive frame on this rung.
sentences.mnemonic: Two verbs, no glue. The second one just stands there in its dictionary clothes.

words.note: To sleep. Its everyday shapes grow a л in the I-form only — сплю (I), спите (you, polite), спит (he or she) — the same quirk M1's люблю had. Russian says Я хочу спать where English says "I'm sleepy".

sentences.trap: не lands in front of хочу, not in front of спать. It denies the wanting, and moving it would deny the sleeping instead.
sentences.sound: ya nye kha-CHOO spat'. Three words lean together into what sounds like two; only хочу carries a real stress.

variations.changed: drop не — and note that this positive version is how Russian says "I'm sleepy"
the person changes and не stays in front of the first verb
swap the second verb — the negation frame takes any of them

mistake.why: That says you want to stay awake. не denies what comes next, so it belongs in front of хочу.

sentences.usage: Turning down a nap, or saying you are not tired — and the positive Я хочу спать is the everyday "I'm sleepy".
sentences.mnemonic: Whatever не touches is what gets denied. Put it where you mean it.

sentences.cue: I want to read a book

words.note: To read, and a very regular verb: читаю (I), читаете (you, polite), читает (he or she) — the endings simply hang off the -а of the stem. M4 uses it as the pattern all the well-behaved verbs follow.

sentences.trap: Both lessons of the module are in this one sentence and they do not interfere: читать stands bare after хочу, and книгу still bends because it is the thing being read. The infinitive does not protect the noun behind it.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO chee-TAT' KNEE-goo. Four unstressed syllables and two stressed ones — Russian rhythm is a series of quick steps and heavy landings.

variations.cue: I want to read a newspaper
variations.changed: swap the thing read — and the new noun bends the same way, because it is feminine too

variations.cue: I don't want to read the book
variations.changed: не in front of the first verb; the other two words do not move

variations.cue: Anna wants to read a book
variations.changed: only хочу changes for the person — the other two words are fixed

mistake.why: книга is still the thing being read, so it still bends: книгу. Standing behind an infinitive changes nothing.

sentences.usage: Saying what you want to do, with what — the fullest sentence this rung can build.
sentences.mnemonic: The infinitive is bare and the noun is bent. Both at once, every time.

words.note: Juice. Masculine, a thing rather than a creature, so it is the same shape everywhere — and short enough to be the easiest word on the rung.

sentences.trap: хотите is the you-form because this course speaks вы — and вы takes the plural ending whether it means one person or a room full of them.
sentences.sound: vy kha-TEE-tye sok. The pitch rises on сок, which is the whole question: nothing was added to make it one.

variations.changed: swap the drink for a feminine one, and the ending appears: воду
хотите → хочу: the answer, with the same unchanged noun
не in front of the verb — in Russian this is an ordinary offer, not a reproach

mistake.why: хочешь is the ты-form, and this course speaks вы. With вы the verb is хотите, however few people you mean.

sentences.usage: Offering something — at a table, in a shop, in somebody's home.
sentences.mnemonic: вы always takes the plural ending. One person, plural verb, every time.

comprehensionPool.cue: I don't want to work, thank you
